---
title: Results
jupyter: python3
---

Every Starsim simulation produces **results**: time series of quantities such as the number of infections, deaths, or people in each disease state. This page explains how results are organized, how to access and manipulate them, and how to plot and export them.

## Where results live

After a sim has run, all of its outputs are stored in `sim.results`, which is a nested structure. Each module adds its own group of results, and there are also some sim-level results (such as `alive`):

```{python}
import starsim as ss
ss.options(jupyter=True)

sim = ss.Sim(n_agents=2000, start='2000', stop='2050', diseases='sir', networks='random', verbose=0).run()

# Top-level groups: one per module, plus sim-level results
print('Result groups:', list(sim.results.keys()))

# The results within the SIR disease module
print('SIR results:  ', list(sim.results.sir.keys()))
```

You access an individual result by drilling down through the module name:

```{python}
new_infections = sim.results.sir.new_infections
print(new_infections)
```

## Anatomy of a result

Each result is an `ss.Result` object. It behaves like a NumPy array (so you can index, slice, and do arithmetic on it directly), but it also carries metadata:

| Attribute | Meaning |
|-----------|---------|
| `values` | The underlying NumPy array of values |
| `timevec` | The time points corresponding to each value |
| `label` | A human-readable label (used in plots) |
| `scale` | Whether the quantity scales with population size (e.g. a count) |
| `kind` | `'flow'` (events in each step), `'stock'` (a number at each time point), or `'ratio'` (one number over another, such as prevalence) |
| `low`, `high` | Optional uncertainty bounds, which `plot()` shows as a band |

```{python}
res = sim.results.sir.new_infections

# Use it like an array
print(f'Peak new infections: {res.max():.0f}')
print(f'Total infections:    {res.sum():.0f}')
print(f'Final timestep:      {res[-1]:.0f}')

# ...but it also knows its own time axis and label
print(f'Label:    {res.label}')
print(f'First date: {res.timevec[0]}')
```

## The results of a declared disease

Every declared disease gets a result for each state and each transition without any being declared: `<state>` (e.g. `I`) is the number of people in the state at each time point (a stock), and each transition has a flow named after it, the number of people who made the transition during each step. A flow's running total is `.cum`. The library's `ss.SIR`, `ss.SIS`, and `ss.SEIR` also keep Starsim's standard names, `new_infections`, `cum_infections`, and `prevalence`:

```{python}
res = sim.results.sir
print('People infected at the end:', res.I[-1])
print('Infections in the last step:', res.infection[-1])
print('Infections so far:', res.infection.cum[-1], 'or', res.cum_infections[-1])
```

Results follow the convention of other modeling frameworks: a result has one value for each time point of the sim, from `start` to `stop`. `I[0]` is the number infected at the start, before any step, and a flow at index 0 is 0, since no step has ended yet; `I[ti]` and `infection[ti]` are the number infected at time point `ti` and the number of infections during the step that ends there. A sim with `stop=T` therefore ends at `T`. (This is one step later than in Starsim 3, where index 0 was the end of the first step.) A flow is dated at the end of its step: with a daily step from `2025-01-01`, the infections dated `2025-02-23` are those during the day that starts on `2025-02-22`, so the peak day of incidence is the day before the date of the largest flow.

```{python}
print('Infected at the start:', res.I[0])
print('Infections at the start:', res.infection[0])
print('Infections in the first step:', res.infection[1])
```

## Declaring more results

Extra results are declared with the model. A sum or ratio of states, given to the disease, is a result (prevalence here); `ss.outcome()` is a reported quantity worked out from flows, here half of infections reported five days later, and hospital admissions with the number in hospital (`n_hosp`):

```{python}
S, I, R = ss.states(3)
N = S + I + R
infection = S >> I @ 0.3 * I
recovery  = I >> R @ ss.days(10)

prevalence = I / N
cases = ss.outcome(0.5 * infection, delay=ss.days(5))
hosp  = ss.outcome(0.05 * infection, delay=ss.days(7), duration=ss.days(10))

model = ss.Disease(
    transitions = [infection, recovery],
    results     = [prevalence],
    outcomes    = [cases, hosp],
    init_prev   = 0.01,
    name        = 'sir',
)
dated = ss.Sim(model, start='2020-01-01', stop='2020-07-01', verbose=0).run()
res = dated.results.sir
print({key: res[key].kind for key in res.keys() if key != 'timevec'})
```

## Changing the time step of a result

Because a result knows whether it is a flow, a stock, or a ratio, converting it to a coarser time step does the right thing without being told: a flow is summed over each period, a stock takes its value at the end of the period, and a ratio is recomputed from its summed parts. `to_series()` returns a pandas series indexed by date:

```{python}
print(res.cases.resample('week').to_series().head())
print(res.I.resample('month').to_series().head())
```

## Results by group

After a disease is stratified (for example by age), each result is still one result, now with a dimension for each stratification. Used as it is, it is the total; `select()` picks groups, and `by()` gives one series per group:

```{python}
by_age = ss.Sim(model.stratify(age=[0, 15, 65], inplace=False), start='2020-01-01', stop='2020-07-01', verbose=0).run()
res_age = by_age.results.sir
print(f'Peak infected: {res_age.I.max():,.0f}, of whom aged 65+: {res_age.I.select(age="65+").max():,.0f}')
print(f'Peak prevalence among children: {res_age.prevalence.select(age="0-14").max():.2f}')
res_age.I.by('age').plot()
```

A ratio such as prevalence is never averaged over groups: its numerator and denominator are each summed over the groups selected, and then divided.

## Data attached by name

Data is attached to results by name: a column called `cases` in a dataframe (or file) given as `data=` is compared with the result `cases`, and plotted with it. Weekly data is compared with the total of a flow over each week. Here the data is made from the model, with noise:

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

weekly = res.cases.to_series(resample='week')
data = pd.DataFrame(dict(date=weekly.index.strftime('%Y-%m-%d'), cases=np.random.default_rng(1).poisson(weekly.values)))
print(data.head())

with_data = ss.Sim(model, data=data, start='2020-01-01', stop='2020-07-01', verbose=0).run()
with_data.plot()
```

A column that matches no result gets a note that lists the closest result names (and is an error when a fit compares the data with the results). Data attached this way is also what [calibration](workflows_calibration.qmd) fits to.

## Plotting results

The quickest way to see everything is `sim.plot()`, which plots all results flagged for automatic plotting:

```{python}
sim.plot()
```

You can plot a single module's results, or even a single result on its own:

```{python}
# Just the SIR results
sim.diseases.sir.plot()
```

```{python}
# A single result, with its label and time axis handled automatically
sim.results.sir.new_infections.plot()
```

## Exporting results

To get results into a pandas dataframe — for example, to save to CSV or analyze further — use `to_df()`. This works at the level of a single module:

```{python}
df = sim.results.sir.to_df()
df.head()
```

or for the whole sim at once, which flattens every module's results into one wide dataframe:

```{python}
df = sim.to_df()
print('Columns:', list(df.columns))
df.head()
```

If you'd rather have a flat dictionary of results keyed by `module_result` (rather than a dataframe), use `sim.results.flatten()`.

## Results across multiple runs

When you run many sims (with [`ss.parallel()`](workflows_run.qmd), or `sim.run(n_runs=...)` for one sim), each result in `msim.results` is the same result as for one sim, with a run axis first. It is summarized over the runs directly:

```{python}
msim = ss.Sim(n_agents=2000, diseases='sir', networks='random', verbose=0).run(n_runs=5)
res = msim.results.sir.new_infections # Runs by time points
print(res.shape)
low, mid, high = res.quantiles([0.1, 0.5, 0.9]) # One series per quantile
res.median() # The median over the runs, as the result of one run
res.select(run=0) # One run
res.plot() # The median and a 95% interval (lines=True for every run)
```

## Results with multiple columns

Sometimes a result in a module written as code naturally has several values per timestep, such as new infections by variant or by age group. (For a declared disease, [stratifying](#results-by-group) does this.) Rather than defining one result per group, you can pass `columns` to `ss.Result`, which makes a 2D result of shape `(npts, ncols)`. In an analyzer, `self.ti` is the time point at the end of the step, where the step's results go, and a declared disease records when each agent was infected (`ti_I`) as the time point at the end of the step in which they were infected:

```{python}
import numpy as np

class InfectionsByAge(ss.Analyzer):
    """ Count new infections among children and adults """
    def init_results(self):
        super().init_results()
        self.define_results(
            ss.Result('new_infections', columns=['children', 'adults'], label='New infections'),
        )

    def step(self):
        new = self.sim.diseases.sis.ti_I == self.ti # Agents who entered I during the step that ends at this time point
        children = self.sim.people.age < 15
        self.results.new_infections[self.ti] = [np.count_nonzero(new & children), np.count_nonzero(new & ~children)]

sim = ss.Sim(n_agents=2000, start=2000, stop=2010, dt=ss.weeks(1), diseases='sis', networks='random', analyzers=InfectionsByAge(), verbose=0).run()
res = sim.results.infectionsbyage.new_infections
print('Shape:', res.shape)
```

Each column is available as a 1D result, via `res.adults` or `res.col('adults')`, or all at once via `res.by_column()`. These share data with the 2D result, so modifying one modifies the other:

```{python}
print(res.adults)
print('Label:', res.adults.label)
print('Columns:', list(res.by_column().keys()))
```

Most operations handle each column separately: results are scaled by `pop_scale`, `to_df()` and `sim.to_df()` give one dataframe column per result column, `sim.summarize()` summarizes each column, and the results of many runs keep the columns (`res.median()` is 2D). Likewise, `resample()` resamples along time only, aggregating by the kind of the parent result (a flow such as `new_infections` is summed, and a stock such as `I` takes its value at the end of each period):

```{python}
annual = res.resample('year')
print('Annual shape:', annual.shape)
annual.to_df().head()
```

Plotting a 2D result shows one line per column:

```{python}
res.plot()
```

## Adding your own results

Any module can define custom results. For one-off analyses, the simplest approach is an [Analyzer](modules_analyzers.qmd); to bake results into a module you're writing, define them with `self.define_results()` (see [Adding new modules](modules_adding.qmd)). Either way, your results are stored in `sim.results` alongside the built-in ones and are exported by `to_df()` automatically.
